description: Ligurian maritime republic (958–1797) that rivalled Venice for Mediterranean commercial supremacy; its network of trading colonies, Caffa in Crimea, Pera in Constantinople, Chios, Famagusta, controlled the luxury goods trade between Asia and Europe, while the Genoese invention of the commenda contract and later the Casa di San Giorgio (1407) pioneered financial instruments adopted across Europe.

temporal.notes: Mediterranean and Black Sea trading republic

lifecycle_phases.description: Genoa declares itself a commune (1099) and rapidly develops as a maritime power. Genoese fleets transport Crusaders and supplies, receiving trading colonies in the Crusader states and Byzantine Empire in return. Competition with Venice and Pisa for Mediterranean trade routes produces the bitter Genoese-Venetian wars. The alliance with Michael VIII Palaiologos at the Treaty of Nymphaion (1261) replaces Venice in the Black Sea trade.

Genoese colonies at Caffa (Crimea), Trebizond, Chios, and throughout the Black Sea make Genoa the dominant force in the luxury trade from the East. Caffa becomes the largest trading post in the world for Chinese goods and Russian furs. The Black Death reaches Europe through Caffa (1347) when Mongol forces catapulted plague-infected corpses over the walls, Genoese ships then spread it to Sicily and Italy.

The War of Chioggia (1378–1381), fought literally within Venice's lagoon, ends in Venetian victory, ending Genoese ambitions of Mediterranean dominance. Genoa retains its Black Sea colonies but loses the initiative. The Ottoman advance eliminates Genoese eastern colonies one by one: Caffa falls (1475). Genoa becomes increasingly subject to Milanese and then French domination.

rise_factors.description: Genoa's treaty with Michael VIII (1261) gave it privileged access to the Black Sea at the expense of Venice; the Caffa colony controlled the northern Silk Road terminus and the Russian fur trade, making Genoa the essential link between Inner Asia and western Europe

Genoa's harbor on the Ligurian coast was the finest in the western Mediterranean for Atlantic-Mediterranean transit; the Ligurian Apennines immediately behind the city provided security against land attack while the sea gave access to all European markets

After the Byzantine alliance of 1261, Genoa dominated Black Sea trade; Caffa (Crimea), Tana (Azov), and Trebizond gave Genoese merchants exclusive access to Central Asian silk, Chinese goods, and eastern European slaves, the most profitable trade in the medieval Mediterranean

The Casa di San Giorgio (founded 1407) was the world's first chartered bank; it managed Genoese public debt, operated colonial taxation, and eventually governed actual territories, the bank became more financially sophisticated than the commune's constitution and outlasted it

Genoese sailors and navigators were employed by foreign rulers from Egypt to Portugal; this diaspora of maritime expertise meant Genoese financial and commercial networks followed wherever Genoese sailors operated, Zaccaria silver alum monopoly (1275), the Maona companies, and eventually Columbus's Castilian voyage

Genoese colonies at Caffa, Soldaia, Tana, and Trebizond gave the republic unrivaled access to the Black Sea trade in grain, furs, slaves, alum, and silk from Central Asia, a commercial empire that persisted even after Constantinople's fall.

decline_factors.description: Ottoman conquest of the Black Sea littoral (culminating in the fall of Caffa, 1475) eliminated Genoa's eastern trading empire; without the Black Sea colonies, Genoa could not compete with Venice's Aegean-based network

The prolonged Genoese-Venetian wars (War of Chioggia, 1378–1381) resulted in Venetian victory and forced Genoa to cede commercial precedence in the Levant; the wars consumed the fiscal reserves that the Bank of Saint George was created partly to manage

Ottoman control of the Bosphorus after 1453 effectively closed the Black Sea to Genoese commerce; Caffa fell to the Ottomans in 1475, eliminating the most profitable node in the Genoese colonial network and forcing Genoese merchants to find new Atlantic routes

Ottoman conquest of Caffa (1475) and the closing of Black Sea trade to Genoese merchants eliminated the commercial foundation of Genoese wealth, forcing the republic to reinvent itself as a banking and financial center under Spanish protection.

sources.author: Wickham, Chris
sources.title: Sleepwalking into a New World: The Emergence of Italian City Communes in the Twelfth Century
